events: An Admonition to the Parliament
John Field and Thomas Wilcox ask Parliament to finish the Reformation: elders in place of bishops. The quarrel over the church’s government begins.
The Marprelate tracts
Anonymous satires on the bishops are printed on a secret press in 1588–1589.
The Art of Prophesying
Perkins sets down the method of the plain sermon: text, sense, doctrine, application.
Hampton Court
James I hears the Puritan ministers’ requests. He grants almost none of them. The exception is a new translation of the Bible (1611).
Plymouth
The Separatists of John Robinson’s church at Leiden sail on the Mayflower.
Massachusetts Bay
Winthrop’s fleet sails. John Cotton preaches God’s Promise to His Plantation at their departure.
Laud at Canterbury
William Laud becomes archbishop. Cotton and Hooker leave for New England the same year.
Prynne, Burton and Bastwick
The three are pilloried and their ears cropped for their writings against the bishops.
The press set loose
Star Chamber is abolished. With the licensing of books in abeyance, pamphlets pour from the London presses.
The Westminster Assembly
Parliament calls divines to Westminster to settle the church. Its work has a guide of its own.
The king executed
Charles I is beheaded in January. The Commonwealth follows.
The Savoy Declaration
The Congregational churches set out their faith and order.
The Great Ejection
Under the Act of Uniformity about two thousand ministers leave their livings on St Bartholomew’s Day.
Toleration
The Act of Toleration allows Protestant Dissenters to worship in their own meeting-houses.

steps: He came to faith by reading. In 1647, ill and expecting to die, he left the army and began The Saints’ Everlasting Rest; it was printed in 1650.
Thirteen years in one parish. He catechized its families one by one, and in The Reformed Pastor (1656) urged the practice on every minister.
At the Savoy Conference of 1661 he pressed the bishops for a reformed liturgy, and lost. The Act of Uniformity of 1662 put him, with about two thousand ministers, out of the Church’s ministry.
Kept from a parish pulpit, he wrote on: A Christian Directory (1673), “a summ of practical theology, and cases of conscience”; Catholic Theology (1675); his Latin Methodus (1681).
In 1685 Judge Jeffreys tried him over his Paraphrase on the New Testament; he was in prison until November 1686, and the line lies flat across those years. He died in London on 8 December 1691.

names.bio: John Lightfoot (1602–1675), born at Stoke-upon-Trent in Staffordshire and died at Ely, was an English biblical scholar and the foremost Christian Hebraist of his generation. Educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, and long rector at Ashley in Staffordshire, he studied rabbinic literature in the conviction that the Talmud and midrashim, whatever their polemical burden, preserve the idiom, geography and institutions that illuminate the New Testament. He sat in the Westminster Assembly from 1643, where his Erastian-leaning interventions on church government and the keys are recorded.
